title: Section 144 — Exploitation of a trafficked person

content.overview: Section 144 — Exploitation of a trafficked person. The operative rule is the text of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body:
144. (1) Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a child has been trafficked, engages such child for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years, but which may extend to ten years , and shall also be liable to fine
(2) Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a person has been trafficked, engages such person for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to seven years , and shall also be liable to fine

learningObjectives: Master the demand-side offence of exploiting a trafficked person under BNS s. 144.
Analyze sub-section (1) penalizing the sexual exploitation of a trafficked child: rigorous imprisonment of five to seven years and fine.
Analyze sub-section (2) penalizing the sexual exploitation of a trafficked adult: rigorous imprisonment of three to five years and fine.
Understand the scienter requirement: knowingly or having reason to believe the person was trafficked.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 144 penalizes the exploitation of a trafficked person: sub-section (1) punishes whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a child has been trafficked, engages such child for sexual exploitation with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than five years but which may extend to seven years, and fine; sub-section (2) punishes whoever engages a trafficked adult for sexual exploitation with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than three years but which may extend to five years, and fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Suppresses human trafficking by criminalizing the demand side, imposing direct penal liability on clients and users who knowingly sexually exploit trafficked victims.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 144 (corresponding to IPC s. 370A).
Sub-section (1): Exploitation of trafficked child — rigorous imprisonment not less than five years extending to seven years, and fine.
Sub-section (2): Exploitation of trafficked adult — rigorous imprisonment not less than three years extending to five years, and fine.
Scienter requirement: 'Knowingly or having reason to believe that the person has been trafficked'.
Substantive act: Engaging the person for sexual exploitation in any manner.
essentialIngredients: The victim is a person who has been trafficked within the meaning of Section 143.
The accused engaged the victim for sexual exploitation in any manner.
The accused knew, or had reason to believe, that the victim was a trafficked person.
For sub-section (1): The victim was a child (under eighteen years).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 144 carries forward IPC 370A. While Section 143 punishes the suppliers and facilitators of trafficking, Section 144 attacks the demand side by penalizing the commercial end-users and customers. It targets anyone who engages a trafficked person for sexual exploitation. The mental element requires proof that the accused knew, or had reason to believe (based on surrounding circumstances such as locked premises, confiscated identity cards, or physical guards), that the person was a trafficked victim. Sub-section (1) applies where the victim is a minor child, mandating rigorous imprisonment of five to seven years. Sub-section (2) applies to adult victims, mandating rigorous imprisonment of three to five years.
examples: Teaching example (Customer of trafficked child): An accused visits an underground brothel, is informed that a fourteen-year-old girl was brought from a neighboring state under duress, and pays money to engage her for sexual acts. The accused is liable under s. 144(1) facing five to seven years rigorous imprisonment.

Teaching example (Client of trafficked adult): An accused engages an adult woman for sexual exploitation while knowing from her pleas that she was brought into the city under false pretences and is held under armed guard. The accused is liable under s. 144(2) (3 to 5 years).
distinctions: Section 144 vs Section 143: Section 143 punishes the recruiter, transporter, or seller; Section 144 punishes the buyer or user who engages the victim for sexual exploitation.
Section 144(1) vs Section 144(2): Sub-section (1) targets child victims (5 to 7 years); Sub-section (2) targets adult victims (3 to 5 years).
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a client who paid a brothel manager for sexual services from a woman who had obvious restraint marks and begged the client for help can claim he did not 'know' she was trafficked.
Rule: Section 144 requires either actual knowledge or 'having reason to believe' that the person was trafficked.
Application: Visible physical restraint and pleas for rescue gave the client ample reason to believe the woman was trafficked.
Conclusion: The client is guilty under BNS s. 144(2).

keyTakeaways: Penalizes clients and users who engage trafficked persons for sexual exploitation.
Requires knowledge or reason to believe the victim was trafficked.
Sub-section (1): Trafficked child (rigorous imprisonment of 5 to 7 years and fine).
Sub-section (2): Trafficked adult (rigorous imprisonment of 3 to 5 years and fine).
